sections.title: What is String Manipulation?
sections.content:
**Strings** are sequences of characters - and in DSA terms, they are essentially arrays of characters. Every array technique applies: traversal, two pointers, prefix tricks, sliding windows. But strings have two critical differences from arrays that change how you code with them.

First, **strings in JavaScript are immutable**. You cannot change a character at position `i` the way you can with `arr[i] = x`. Every operation that appears to modify a string - concatenation, slice, replace - creates a **new string**. This means repeated `str += char` in a loop allocates a new string each iteration: O(1) + O(2) + O(3) + ... + O(n) = O(n²) total. The fix: push characters into an array and join at the end.

Second, strings have **semantic structure** that pure arrays don't. Characters have frequencies. Words have palindrome symmetry. Two strings can be anagrams. Recognizing these properties and choosing the right data structure to exploit them - typically a frequency map - is the core skill of string problems.

The most important string problem archetypes are: **anagram detection** (frequency map), **palindrome problems** (two pointers), **substring problems** (sliding window), and **string parsing** (traversal with state). Each has a canonical template that you should be able to write from memory.

sections.title: When to Use This
sections.content: String techniques apply to any problem where the input is text and the answer depends on the content or structure of that text. Frequency maps are the right tool when 'rearrangement' or 'anagram' appears. Two pointers are right for palindrome verification. Sliding window is right for 'longest or shortest substring with a property'. Whenever the problem says 'contiguous characters meeting a condition', sliding window is likely optimal.
signals: find a substring with a given property
check if two strings are anagrams
palindrome check or longest palindromic substring
rearrange characters to meet a condition
count occurrences of a character or pattern
minimum window containing all required characters

sections.title: Character Frequency Maps
Two Pointers on Strings
Substring Problems and Sliding Window
sections.content:
The **brute force** for substring problems: try all O(n²) substrings, check each in O(n) → O(n³) total. Even with O(1) check, O(n²) substrings is too slow for large inputs.

**Sliding window** reduces this to O(n) by maintaining a window of characters and updating its state incrementally as the window moves. The window has two pointers: `left` and `right`. `right` always advances by 1 each outer step. `left` advances only when the window violates the constraint.

For 'longest substring without repeating characters': maintain a frequency map of window contents. When a character's frequency exceeds 1, shrink from the left until it doesn't.

## Window State Tracking

Simple windows track a sum or a count. Complex windows track:
- A frequency map of characters in the window
- A count of 'satisfied' character requirements (for minimum window substring)
- The number of distinct characters currently in the window

The shrink step must always mirror the expand step: if expanding increments a counter, shrinking must decrement it.

sections.title: Efficient String Building
Core Template
sections.explanation: The frequency map template handles any character-counting task. The sliding window template shows the expand-right / shrink-left pattern: right advances every iteration, left advances only when the constraint (here: distinct characters > k) is violated. Adapt the constraint and the window state to any substring problem.

items.name: Multiline String Processing
items.description: Splitting by newline (`s.split('\n')`), processing each line, then joining is the pattern for multiline inputs. Each line is a separate string; treat it as an independent substring problem. Common in text editor and log-parsing problems.

items.name: String Compression (Run-Length Encoding)
items.description: Scan the string with a pointer, count consecutive identical characters, output the character followed by its count. Two-pointer variant: read pointer `i` advances through repeats, write pointer `w` writes compressed output back into the same array.

items.name: Pattern Matching
items.description: Finding a pattern string inside a text. Brute force is O(n*m). KMP algorithm reduces to O(n+m) using a prefix-suffix table. For interview purposes, JavaScript's `text.indexOf(pattern)` is fine, but knowing KMP conceptually shows depth.
items.example_problem: Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String

sections.title: Complexity
sections.time: O(n) for frequency maps and sliding window, O(n²) brute force substring
sections.space: O(k) for sliding window where k is alphabet size or distinct character count
sections.explanation: A frequency map is built in one pass - O(n). Sliding window's right pointer advances n times and left pointer advances at most n times total (not per right step) - O(n) overall despite the nested while loop. Space is O(k) for the frequency map where k is the number of distinct characters in the window, bounded by the alphabet size (26 for lowercase English).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Using `==` for string comparison where case sensitivity matters: `'A' == 'a'` is `false`, but easy to forget when transforming strings. Always clarify case sensitivity, and use `.toLowerCase()` if case-insensitive comparison is needed before storing in a frequency map.

`str.split('').reverse().join('')` silently corrupts strings with Unicode surrogate pairs: emoji like '😀' are encoded as two UTF-16 code units, and `split('')` splits them apart. For ASCII-only strings this is fine, but mention the limitation if the problem discusses Unicode.

Confusing `substring`, `slice`, and `substr`: `str.substr(start, length)` is deprecated. `str.substring(start, end)` treats negative indices as 0 and swaps start/end if start > end. `str.slice(start, end)` handles negatives correctly (counts from end). Always use `slice`.

Case sensitivity gotcha in frequency map keys: storing 'A' and 'a' as separate keys when the problem is case-insensitive doubles the map size and makes anagram checks wrong. Normalize to lowercase before building the frequency map.

Forgetting to delete from Map when frequency reaches zero: in a sliding window with a `Map`, a key with value 0 still exists in the map and is counted in `map.size`. Call `map.delete(key)` when its count drops to 0, or `map.size` will overcount distinct elements.

items.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
items.why: The canonical variable-size sliding window problem - tests the expand-right / shrink-left pattern with a frequency map.

items.title: Longest Palindromic Substring
items.why: Tests expand-around-center technique - for each position, expand outward while characters match, tracking the longest found.

items.title: Valid Anagram
items.why: Direct application of character frequency map - the simplest and most foundational string problem.

items.title: Minimum Window Substring
items.why: The most complex sliding window variant - requires tracking how many required characters are fully satisfied, not just present.

sections.title: What to Learn Next
sections.why: Sliding window is the formalization of the technique you've been using for substring problems - learning it as a standalone pattern lets you apply it to array problems, not just strings, and introduces the fixed-size window variant.
